implementation_notes: The broker is the durable store: receive in PeekLock mode so the message stays locked and is redelivered when the lock expires, process, and settle with CompleteMessageAsync only after the business commit; AbandonMessageAsync releases the lock immediately and DeadLetterAsync parks a poison message. Exactly-once is completed on the send side by duplicate detection, which drops a second message with the same application-controlled MessageId inside the detection window - which is what makes a client retry after an unknown send outcome safe. Choose this variant for cloud workloads; MSMQ (below) is the local store when no cloud broker is allowed.
pitfalls: Settling after the receiver or connection was closed: the settlement never reaches the service, the lock expires and the message is redelivered - then repeated redelivery moves it to the dead-letter queue.
A lock duration shorter than the processing time (renew with RenewMessageLockAsync or use sessions), and a MaxDeliveryCount that turns a bug into silent dead-lettering.
Duplicate detection considers only the MessageId: a fresh GUID per attempt defeats it, and the detection window (default 10 minutes) bounds how long a replay stays safe.
Non-idempotent handlers: PeekLock is at-least-once, so a lock expiry after a successful business effect duplicates that effect.

variants.name: MSMQ transactional queue (local store, DTC-enlisted)
variants.implementation_notes: Windows-local realization with its own transactional log: a queue created with Transactional = true journals sends and receives, so a send becomes durable on commit and a receive that is not committed returns the message to the queue (the automatic redelivery the pattern needs). Enlisting the queue together with a database connection in one DTC transaction is what makes 'business write plus send' atomic without an outbox table. This is .NET Framework-era technology: the modern equivalents are a broker (Service Bus above) or a transactional outbox, and the classic form is justified mainly in on-premises Windows estates that already run MSMQ.
pitfalls: Recoverable = true is required for the message body to survive a reboot; a transactional queue alone only makes the operation atomic, not the payload persistent.
Distributed transactions need the DTC service, are slow, and make the send path fail whenever DTC or the database's XA support is unavailable.
System.Messaging exists only on .NET Framework/Windows (MSMQ cannot be used from .NET Core without a client library), so the variant is not portable.
A non-transactional Receive inside a transaction context silently bypasses the journal, and the message is lost when the process dies after processing but before ack.
